Atlantic provinces, we must also find the additional oil that is going to be needed to supply all of Canada's needs in the future. We know that today Quebec and the Atlantic provinces together use some 900,000 barrels of oil per day, which when the pipeline to Montreal is finally completed in some two to three years will amount at least to an additional one million barrels a day that have to be found.
Where is that extra oil going to come from? Obviously, most of that oil has not yet been discovered. We must find this additional oil because we cannot in any way interfere with the one million barrels a day of oil and the 250,000 barrels a day of petroleum products which we deliver by contract to the United States. I think it is obvious to all members of this House and to all Canadians that any attempt to do divert even a small part of that solemnly entered into commitment would have a catastrophic effect both on our trading relationships with the United States, where we export 70 per cent of all our export products, and on our general relationship, on which we rely so heavily, with our neighbour to the south. In order to have enough oil to look after our needs for the future, we will have to discover two barrels of new oil per day for each barrel that we use. If we do not discover new oil at this rate, in ten years we are going to start running out of this fuel.
Let us ask ourselves how we have been doing in this regard in recent years. The sad story is that during the past three years we have discovered only one new barrel for each barrel of oil that we have been using. So the next question is: Where must we find the additional oil we are going to need? The answer, of course, is that it must come mostly from three places, the Arctic islands, the Mackenzie delta, and off the east coast of Canada.
The next question is: How much money should we be spending each year on exploration to produce both our present needs and the additional oil we are going to need in the future? The answer to that given by the oil industry, the people who have to do the discovering, and the only people who are doing this discovery work now, is that we must spend in the future a minimum of $750 million a year. The present indication is that, because of the lack of confidence that the oil industry has in the policies of this government, the amount of money that will be spent next year, 1974, will be only about half of this $750 million. This, of course, will leave this country very, very short of the oil we are going to need, and we must do something about it.
The reason this discovery process is being slowed down so materially is that the oil industry on which we have to rely to find this new oil is very, very dissatisfied with the decision-making process of this government. Unless they can get the decisions that must be made by this government in the very near future, we will be very short of the oil we will need in the future.
What are the oil companies trying to find out? First of all, they want to find out-and have been waiting for 2 Vi years to get this information, with no result whatsoever- the federal government's stand on the question of permits, leases and royalties in respect of Arctic and offshore oil that will be discovered as a result of the exploratory

programs of the oil industry. Until these answers are given to the petroleum industry, the companies which will be putting up the risk capital to do this work in discovery of new petroleum will not spend any more than the projected amount I have given, that is, $375 million in 1974 instead of twice that amount, $750 million, which is the amount that must be spent if we are to find new oil now to enable this country to become self-sufficient in the future.
The government must make up its mind on what it intends to do regarding these matters, and let the oil companies know just what that intention is. It must sit down and discuss these matters with the oil industry and work out mutually satisfactory solutions. When it does that, the oil companies will go out and spend this $750 million. They want to do this and are anxious to do it, but they will not do it until they find out from this government how it intends to treat the finds they make at great cost to themselves. I think we all agree that is a very fair stand for the petroleum industry.
The second thing that has held back the production of additional oil products is the lack of a decision to go ahead with the Athabasca tar sands. This afternoon the Prime Minister spoke glibly about the way this project is going to go forward. It is not going to go forward until the Syncrude Corporation is advised by this government that it is willing to treat the 50 per cent net profit, that portion which by agreement will accrue to the Alberta government, in exactly the same way as any other royalty paid to any other government, for tax purposes, by the federal government. When the Syncrude Corporation is advised that this government is willing to treat 50 per cent of the net profits in that way, then the Syncrude project will go forward. It will not go forward until the federal government makes that information available. It is as simple as that. The Prime Minister can make all the syrupy speeches he wants, trying to build confidence in this country, about how this big project is going ahead; but I tell you it will not go ahead until this government gets off the seat of its pants, does a little thinking and lets the oil industry know what it is going to do in respect of this important matter.
Something that should disturb all of us who are interested in the provision of fuel for this country, and who are particularly interested in the magnificent Syncrude project, is information that the United States government has just issued the first six permits required to develop the oil shales of Colorado. This is a similar type of project to the Athabasca tar sands. If this project gets into production before the Syncrude project, this may very easily diminish very considerably the value of the Athabasca tar sands.
The oil industry in Canada is very worried about this aspect of the whole proposition, but the government does not seem to pay any attention to this concern. It seems to think we have the Athabasca tar sands production all to ourselves, it can do what it wants and take all the time it wants. Those in the oil industry who know of this matter will tell you that the Colorado oil shales represent a very worrying aspect of this whole matter. For that reason, this government should make a decision and so advise the Syncrude Corporation, allowing that very important resource to be developed in the shortest possible time.
Finally, the petroleum industry in Canada is holding back on the expansion of its operations because the gov-
December 6, 1973

ernment has largely removed from the National Energy Board the advisory function that was definitely granted it by the National Energy Board Act when it was passed in 1959. In the years following the passing of that act, the oil and gas industry learned to have great confidence in the recommendations of that board because those recommendations were based upon facts and not on political considerations. These facts and recommendations were made known to the oil and gas industry. The government, of course, had the right to decide on oil policy. But when the National Energy Board had the right to advise the government and make that advice known to the oil and gas industry, the industry knew the government was making these decisions, whatever they may be, on the basis of facts and not just on the basis of political considerations.
The government's oil policy today is decided 100 per cent in this way. What bothers the oil industry so much today is that these decisions are not only political but, as we have seen in the last few weeks, they can be changed two or three times in a single week. When an industry requires up to eight years from the time the decision to develop a project is made until the final production of the oil and gas, one can understand why such an industry cannot have any confidence in decisions based on political considerations, as they are now, and changed as rapidly as are the decisions of this government.
The speech made by the Prime Minister today is the greatest example of how the decisions of this government can change almost daily. His speech contained assertions that the government intends to do those things which a few days or weeks ago it stated flatly, over and over again, it would not do. Now, because the party to the left, the NDP, put the heat on and said it would defeat the government on Monday night if it did not come to terms and do exactly what that party wanted done, the Prime Minister has changed his mind. His speech could easily have been written by the hon. member for York South. My information is that that member did have a great deal to do with the writing of this speech. One thing that has been proved beyond any shadow of a doubt is that in the future Canada is going back to the two-party system; there will be a free enterprise party and a socialist party.
Both the Liberal Party and the NDP have a very celebrated day-December 6, 1973. It is going to be known as "A" day, amalgamation day. They will celebrate it together. There will be bonfires burning in their caucuses tonight, and everybody will be very very happy indeed.

Those are the words of Darcy McKeough, the minister of energy in the province of Ontario. Here we have a national Conservative Party that wants to take price controls off energy in the country and allow the price to float in relation to what the international price may be, whatever it may be. I do not wish to comment on the statement the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made today, except to say one of the significant things in it is that we now have some public involvement in the oil industry in this country. How much that may be will be seen some time in the future.
We must take this energy situation very seriously. It is an important issue, not just for now but for the future of this country. We must have a policy which includes not only price but also those who own and control the industry in this country. To us in this party, this is very important. We suggest there should be public ownership of the energy resources of this country and that, like electricity, any energy should be treated as a public utility and should not be left solely in the hands of national and international cartels.
I suggest that the announcement made by the Prime Minister today is the beginning of some kind of public involvement in the gas industry in Canada. But I would

like to see all future energy resources in this country treated as a public utility, under public ownership, through joint co-operation between the various provinces and the federal government. I can assure you that some provinces would be very interested in that type of proposal.
The development of energy resources could be financed through public ownership quite easily. For example, we could channel the revenues from the export tax, which will amount to millions of dollars annually if the situation remains as it is, into the development of energy resources for the public. If there is to be a price increase some time in the future, we could earmark the increase over the cost of the oil industry toward the development of that industry under public ownership.
These are just a couple of proposals regarding the future development of gas and oil in this country. Many people in this House have heard complaints that the oil industry does not have enough incentives. A few minutes ago the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) said that the oil industry does not have the confidence of this country and therefore it will not develop. I wonder why they say that. All they have to do is look at the profit picture for the last year to see whether or not the oil industry has enough incentive.
First of all, we find that the price per barrel that the oil industry receives has gone up by 95 cents in 1973. That is an increase of 37 per cent that the oil companies are getting. This is before any kind of price freeze or export tax has been levied by the government. This increase that the government has granted them has brought the oil companies some $700,000 this year, and some companies have had profits of some 87 per cent. I suggest that that is a hefty increase for the oil companies and a real incentive, as the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) said. I think the time has come when there must be public control and public ownership of the energy resources of our country.
I think, for example, that the price control to which the Prime Minister referred regarding energy should not be lifted at the end of next April but should be a permanent part of the energy policy of this country, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) said in the House yesterday. There is no reason at all why there should not be some permanent price controls on energy in this country, which would be adjusted only when the oil companies have legitimate increases in cost. And the price should not be adjusted to give the oil industry additional profits.

That is an idea to which this party wants to hold the Prime Minister when he refers to unnecessary profiteering by the gas and oil industry. It is a selective control that our party is advocating. It is not like the phony 90-day freeze that the Conservative Party is advocating on commodities, on wages and prices across this country. That would not help anyone; it would only hurt the pensioner and the low income earner.
I also suggest that the export tax be a permanent feature of our gas and oil policy. If there are any windfall gains to be made in the gas and oil industry, those gains should
December 6, 1973

come back to the people of this country who own the resources, not to some foreign-based, multinational corporations. The windfall gains that are made could be channelled into a fund, for example into the Canadian Development Corporation for the development of the tar sands, the development of the resources in the north and in other parts of this country under public ownership, so the people of Canada could reap the benefits, rather than the few entrepreneurs who live outside our borders.
All one has to do is look at some of the real effects that foreign ownership has had in our oil industry to realize the emergency proportion it has reached. I find that over $1 billion is leaving Canada this year in terms of dividends and profits from the oil industry and finding its way into the hands of foreign investors, perhaps in the United States. Much of that $1 billion is used for exploration outside of this country, such as in the North Sea. Another statistic I have is that about 86 per cent of the dividends on the earnings made by oil corporations in this country go outside of Canada, and only 14 per cent stay here for exploration, development and expansion. In my opinion, that is an example of the negative value of foreign ownership and control.
It is not only that. When you have that type of control of the oil industry, you find there is a lack of jobs. For example, the petrochemical industry is not developed in Canada, but elsewhere. This is one of the by-products of foreign ownership. You will find that in times of emergency, such as we have now, an oil corporation may divert some of its supplies from one destination to another. Multinational oil companies are huge international private governments; they are huge elephants that stamp around in countries as if those countries were small ants scurrying to get out of the way of the big feet of the elephant. In the House we have a perfect lobby for these companies, namely, the Progressive Conservative Party. We should tell the people of Canada about it as loudly, as clearly and as often as we possibly can.
I think we should do all we can to force the government of this country to become more and more involved in the gas and oil industry on behalf of the people of Canada, because that industry belongs to the people and we have the money, technology and resources to develop it. Therefore, we should develop it for the use of the Canadian people. If we do that, Canada might have a great future, because there is a genuine shortage of energy throughout the world and if Canada developed its own energy industry this could have a real spin-off effect in other industries. Countries in western Europe, countries like Japan, Great Britain and perhaps the United States, will want to import more manufactured goods and have a high energy input some time in the future.
If we in Canada have our own energy resources and an abundant supply of them at the cheapest possible price, we will be able to produce more goods for export to other countries that might be less fortunate in terms of gas and oil. I suggest it is important that we keep pushing the government now and in the future toward getting more involved in the gas and oil industry of this country. As I said, I think we can do it. I think we should be encouraging the government now to buy out the major oil companies. If we did that, we would be on the way to real public
Energy Supplies Emergency Act involvement in the gas and oil industry. If we expanded and used the export tax, the tax revenues on gas and oil, we would have in this country within 10 or 15 years an energy industry wholly owned by the people. We would not have to take over the oil companies. In 10 or 15 years their assets would be depleted and they would be a public utility, under public control and ownership, a people's oil industry that would serve the people of this country. Any profits that were made would stay here, and any oil man will tell you that the oil industry today is very profitable, for they are raking in literally millions and millions of dollars.
Any decisions that were made would then be made here in Canada for the public good, not the private good, and any jobs created in the petroleum industry would be here in Canada. We could develop an industrial structure that was responsive to our needs both social and economic. The bill we are debating today, I see as a small part in the national energy policy that this country should be evolving in the next 12 or 15 years.
The allocation bill we have before us will give the government some of the powers to take the steps that I and others in my party want taken, and that I suggest the people of the country want taken. A Gallup poll conducted a few months ago showed that the majority of the people of the country want the energy resources of the country, including gas and oil, brought under public ownership and control. It also showed that the Liberals and Conservatives surveyed preferred to have energy resources owned by the people rather than by foreign-based, multinational corporations. That is the direction in which we should be moving. We can move in that direction. Other countries have done so and there is no reason why Canada should not.
We have the resources, Mr. Speaker. In the oil sands of Alberta and Saskatchewan we have in oil reserves as much as all of the Arab states put together. We should not allow the tar sands to be sold out in the same way that the oil industry to date has been sold out to foreigners. As a result, the oil policy of this country has been established by foreign-based, multinational corporations in the private sector. The time has come to change that policy and have a public input on behalf of the people of the country.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I started off by saying I am delighted with the statement made by the Prime Minister today, indicating in no uncertain terms that the government intends to exercise control over the development of our natural resources and to see that the corporations, multinational or otherwise, act in such a way as to maximize protection for the consumer, particularly the consumer of home heating oil products.
Bill C-236 clearly restates our desire to have complete control over emergency supply allocations in Canada and is a welcome move. It is an emergency step to deal with the emergency situation in which we now find ourselves, but if passed by parliament it will be available as a permanent piece of legislation for use in any other such emergencies in times to come. The broad powers provided under the bill are necessary in order to protect our economy, the essential services of the country, and more particularly the oil consumer in terms of supply and prices.
It will also protect something that is very close to the hearts and minds of all Canadians, in that the independent distributors of petroleum products can now be assured that they will not be squeezed out of the marketplace by the multinational corporations who may have a vested interest in serving themselves rather than the independent dealers with whom they were happy to deal in the past.
Through this bill we are also ensuring the best use of our distribution system-ship, rail, truck and pipeline-to see that the private sector behaves in a good corporate way in meeting the national objective of getting energy supplies to all Canadians and to the essential public services which require them. Of course, at a time of crisis and high demand we must hedge the public against what might be termed corporate greed, against the self-interest of the multinationals who can arbitrarily dislocate the economy and national well-being of our citizens at large. This crisis has provided Canada with a tremendous opportunity to act now and dramatically exert national control over multinational corporations to make sure they serve the best interests of all Canadians, and to ensure that for years to come, for centuries to come, this country will be self-sufficient in energy supplies.
The Prime Minister spoke not only in terms of oil supplies but in terms of delivery systems. However, Bill C-236, now before the House is directed more toward

delivery than supply. There is no question that supplies are a problem of a worldwide nature, and in particular for developing countries. It was interesting that the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) did not seem to recognize this point, and I gather that the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) does not recognize it either.
The hon. member, speaking of supplies, talked about the Syncrude project and indicated that as a result of the Americans going forward with their shale development project in the United States this might well lessen the value of our tar sands unless we develop them rather quickly. To me, this implies a feeling on his part that once these two projects are developed we will have a world surplus of oil then and in the future. That flies directly in the face of the well known fact that, with the passage of time, the world will still be in an energy crisis and alternative energy supplies must be developed. I do not know how the Conservatives can have it both ways, one talking about the tremendous energy crisis and another saying we had better hurry up the development of tar sands because, if we do not, the Americans will beat us with their shale project and therefore we will not have anything worth while in Canada. That does not seem to be at all consistent.
Another matter with respect to the rather nebulous position of the Conservative Party in regard to this overall problem is the fact that during the 1972 election campaign, and afterwards, I was under the impression that the Conservatives were the party who wanted to have wage and price controls. The simple fact now is that every time controls are put on one sector of the economy or another by the government in order to protect the consumers, the Conservatives cry "foul". Their leader, when in Vancouver the other day, indicated that when the petroleum price freeze is lifted he would like to see staged increases. That does not sound very consistent to me.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister responded properly, f thought, by saying that we would keep controls on and see that the best interests of all Canadians are protected. I welcome the establishment of the Canadian petroleum corporation because I think it is essential for the Canadian government to involve itself in exploration in conjunction with the private sector. I particularly welcome the emphasis the Prime Minister gave to.our supporting and helping, in exploration activities, those smaller Canadian-owned petroleum corporations which find it difficult to compete with the large multinational corporations. I think that will do much to help give us a greater degree of Canadian control over our natural resources.
The Prime Minister mentioned the pipeline from the west to the Montreal area. That is very important. I am delighted with the urgent priority given to this matter. May I make a suggestion, which is not really original to myself, which might be considered. In the interim, at the appropriate time we might be able to take advantage of some of the excellent personnel in the armed forces who could help in the development of this project and speed it up.
I think the new Canadian petroleum corporation could be used as a vehicle for development. Under its aegis we could set up a development fund into which special taxes and depletion allowances as presently available to the

December 6, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
large oil companies in this country could be funnelled, so that we could establish a sizeable fund for developing our own natural resources, which would include not only the tar sands but offshore resources and resources in other parts of Canada.
The oil export tax, established in Canada some months ago over the cries of "foul" by many Conservative members, I think has been a useful tool for ensuring that the government of Canada, in conjunction with the government of Alberta, can build up funds for those very developmental purposes. The export tax which many were led to believe was a tax against the consumers of Canada is in fact a tax to protect them. It was to make sure that people in Canada are only paying Canadian prices, not prices according to the Chicago market. Because of the export tax there has been a considerable increment in funds to be used for national purposes such as the development of oil projects in future. I welcome that.
Many Canadians are not fully aware of the enormous rise in the price of oil which has taken place in the world, and how much we have to be thankful for in this country because we are not permitting international prices to be charged on the domestic market. Recently, for instance, Nigerian oil has been sold for $16.40 per barrel; Tunisian oil for $12.60 per barrel. The Chicago market price, as best I can calculate, with our tax added is $6.40 per barrel. The Canadian price is much lower than that, being in the neighbourhood of $4 per barrel, only because the government has put the lid on and made sure that the corporations do not line their pockets because of the international energy crisis.
Another area that concerns me a great deal is the need for us to develop and stimulate alternative sources to fossil fuel for energy purposes. A good example of what we can do has taken place in my own constituency. For example, the Prime Minister referred to the Pickering nuclear plant. That has been a phenomenal success, something of which all Canadians can be proud. It is much more successful than any alternative form of developing hydroelectric power tried by any other country in the world, including the United States. The fact that it uses uranium rather than enriched uranium causes a greatly reduced operating cost of that plant.
I welcome the suggestion by the Prime Minister that the federal government will participate, as it did in the Pickering project, in developing similar plants in the provinces across Canada. By doing this, the impact can be phenomenal in terms of reduced fossil fuel use. For example, the Pickering plant is at present capable of generating enough power to heat every home in Toronto and light every light at peak periods. All this can be done by one nuclear plant. That is quite an achievement.
I think in the long haul we ought to give more emphasis to this kind of energy and less to the conversion of homes to the use of natural gas and oil supplies for home heating purposes, particularly in large metropolitan areas like Toronto, Montreal, and so on. It is now proposed to double the plant in Pickering. After that is completed, it will generate an enormous amount of power. It will take some of the pressure off the use of fossil fuels. I am sure it will

serve as an enormous export boon when the world becomes aware, as it has increasingly been doing, of the tremendous project we have in the Pickering generating station.
There are other things we must do, perhaps in conjunction with the United Nations or at least other countries. We should evolve massive projects by numbers of countries in the world to look into the problems of solar energy. This is enormously expensive to develop. We must develop hydrogen use and other forms of energy production. There is no question that in 20 or 30 years, which is not long in the lifetime of a nation or the world, we will have to look at these other sources. I believe Canada can set the pace and an example in the development of that kind of approach in which we will conserve our energy, keeping it for a longer period of time in areas where it is really essential and not using it in areas where alternatives are presently available.
The same is true with regard to the use of automobiles. On a recent trip to England, I was quite impressed with a milk van which, when full, carried 40 cases of milk. It was powered by electricity, two batteries, one on each side of the vehicle. It travelled over 50 miles an hour, with a range of 250 miles on one charge. It is plugged in at night and then used for a full day for the delivery of this product. I do not know why there is not more emphasis given in this country to that clean form of operation for delivery vehicles. Even with its limited use, it can certainly be used much more extensively than at the present time.
Energy is a long and involved subject. I am delighted that the government, through the speech of the Prime Minister today, illustrated its determination to control this field and see that the consumers of Canada are protected, in terms of delivery and supply, in both the short run and the long run and are protected in terms of price so that they will not be gouged now or in the future because of artificial pressures and shortages that have been created.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to get the debate back on the rails, may I point out that this is a second reading debate on Bill C-236. I think members opposite have lost track of what this debate is about. I was rather surprised today with the panic of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government over this crisis. It is really a government crisis and not an energy crisis. The Prime Minister's statement has been called a new national oil policy. There was not anything new about it. We have heard on several occasions the same announcements he made today. However, there was one that struck me forcibly. I will call it as a witness in my opening remarks. I will name the witness. It is very interesting. It is a very fresh piece of evidence. This is what the witness said: "It means that the cost of producing domestic oil must go up before too long. It means that Canadians must be prepared, sooner or later, in some way or another to pay for these additional costs or go without oil. Representatives of the industry came to Ottawa in 1969 and begged the government to take action to see that a pipeline was built so that Canada's oil supply would always be secure. What really happened was this: they relied on imports. Nobody wanted western Canadian crude petroleum for years. We couldn't give it away. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), when he led off this debate for our party, described the board as owned, operated and manned by the minister. This board is being conceived in an atmosphere of failure of decision on the part of the government. It is being conceived in the climate of a desperate minority government clinging to power. It is being conceived at a time when the government wishes to bury its procrastination or, at least, to have its procrastination interpreted as Liberal pragmatism and action.
It is a great disappointment to me, and I know it is a great disappointment to all western Canadians who realize that Canada has become self-sufficient as far as energy supplies are concerned, to find that the government cannot use its power as it ought to be used because of deals with its NDP friends. What is really happening is this. We have an NDP government with a rump on the other side directing the policies of the government, both parties standing, speaking and voting together and planning a socialistic state.
Once this board is set up, all-powerful and all-encompassing, the minister-I can almost hear him now-will answer questions put to him in reference to autocratic and arbitrary decisions, or decisions which are wrong and unjust, by saying these are decisions of the board. It is the board, he will tell us, which made those decisions. He will pass the buck to the board while he himself dons the veil of innocence. I have no doubt that the board will be used as a political vehicle and as an instrument for granting privileges to favoured political areas while creating adversity for others. It really is a super-department set up under the control of the minister to carry out his will as if he were a general in the field fighting a battle.

One has only to examine the grants made by the Liberal Party under the LIP program to know that the government cannot be trusted and will continue along this road of being political and partisan to the extent of being irresponsible. Once you give the minister the power that this bill gives to him, he will make decisions in one province which may be very favourable because the political climate is very favourable to him in that province. But he will make other decisions in other provinces which do not vote Liberal, just as the LIP program was a political slush-fund for Liberal interests and Liberal candidates everywhere.

This board has the power to act on a regional basis, as is apparent when you read the sections of the bill. I imagine they could ration gas and oil in Alberta and remove rationing in other provinces which do not even produce the commodity. If they can do what they did to the LIP program, then they can manoeuvre as far as the energy program is concerned.
Let me give a few examples of the sections contained in the bill. Clause 15 gives the minister power over provincial rights to control all energy and fuel, even electric power. I wonder what the province of Quebec will say when they find that by clause 15 of this bill the government, through this board, can step in, take over electrical energy and the hydro plant of Quebec, direct how it will be operated, direct the price, direct the imports and exports, and direct and control the operation itself. If that is not an infringement of provincial rights, nothing is.
Let me refer to clause 17(4) and clause 18(4), at pages 11 and 12 of the bill. What do they say? Let me just show the House what the bill does say. Clause 17 deals with the regulation of imports and subsection (4) provides:
In the event of a conflict between any regulation under this act and any provision of the National Energy Board Act or any regulation made thereunder, the regulation under this act prevails.
In other words, the National Energy Board, which was set up as a quasi-judicial body to make independent decisions on supply, to control supply, to control imports, to control exports, to give inventories of energy supplies from time to time, is having its jurisdiction taken away by this board whose only power lies under the direction of the general, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
December 6, 1973

What does clause 18 have to say? After all, we are debating this bill. It says:
(4) In the event of a conflict between any regulation under this Act and any provision of the National Energy Board Act or any regulation made thereunder, the regulation under this act prevails.
This section is dealing with regulating exports, obtaining an inventory and sizing up the situation as between imports and exports. When this bill is passed it will permit the minister to veto any decision of the National Energy Board, which as I say was set up as an independent board and has worked very well since it came into operation in 1962. It is interesting also to look at clause 21. Hon. members talk about civil rights. Clause 21, at page 14 of the bill, provides:
Where pursuant to a regulation under this Act any person is required to do or to omit to do anything contrary to the terms and conditions of any contract entered into by that person, the contract is modified to the extent necessary to enable compliance to be made with the requirements of the regulation.
In other words, any contracts made between corporations or people as far as natural gas, crude petroleum or other forms of energy are concerned can be altered or changed by the minister at will for his power lust. This is part of the bill we are asked to approve. The strongest provision comes on page 15. I often wonder, when I listen to some people, if they ever read the bills they are talking about. Clause 23 gives the minister this power. It provides:
Where in order to comply with any regulation under this act a person would be required to enter into any agreement, arrangement or course of action that might cause him to contravene the Combines Investigation Act, such person may apply to the board for an order exempting him from that act in respect of that particular agreement, arrangement or course of action.
In other words, this bill gives the minister the right to allow people to enter into contracts contrary to the Combines Investigation Act and do away with all competition. What will the result be? If that does not result in higher prices to the consumer, then no terms or conditions or any act would. As I see it, that is the effect of the bill.
I have spoken of some of the weaknesses of the bill as I see the situation. The Prime Minister spoke this afternoon, and one of the questions we have to analyse is his credibility and the credibility of the minister. Today, if I heard him aright, and hon. members can check his speech, he said that 50 per cent of the surtax would go back to the provinces. Not only have I at the committee level but also in this House of Commons questioned the minister and the Prime Minister about this, but I have been assured by the minister not only in the House but at the committee level that 100 per cent of the tax would go back to the producing province. I should like to refer to report No. 44 of the miscellaneous estimates committee where this question was asked by me, and later by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). The hon. member asked:
Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if the minister could clarify a statement that he made earlier with respect to the $1.90 per barrel tax. Did I understand him correctly to say that either directly or indirectly the entire tax will go back either to the province or be used within the province where it originated?

Yes, sir.
So we were promised by the minister that 100 per cent of that tax would go back to Alberta or Saskatchewan where the crude petroleum is produced, passing through the
Energy Supplies Emergency Act Interprovincial pipeline into eastern Canada. Yet today the Prime Minister vetoed the statement of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources with reference to the return of that tax to the provinces.
Not only will this bill override provincial rights. Once you give the government this power they will certainly override provincial rights, particularly in a province that does not support the Liberal Party. This puts me in mind of Mackenzie King's slogan during the depression. He said, "There won't be one five-cent piece for any unemployed person in any province where there is a Conservative government". Those words came to haunt him in the 1930 election.
Therefore, it is now obvious that Canada's so-called energy crisis is one of absence of government leadership and responsibility in energy matters. This is becoming more apparent every day as the government continues on a course that seems to be not only lacking in solutions but in a clear understanding of what action has taken place. Canada this winter is faced with a major petroleum supply shortage in eastern Canada and the Maritimes. All of this is due to a lack of planning of our transportation facilities. I shall never tire of repeating that this pipeline should have been built and be in operation by now. There would not have been any shortage of fuel or gasoline in this country today if it had. We have the crude petroleum and natural gas, plus other energy commodities, to be totally self-sufficient, but the pipeline capacity is inadequate, as the government is now finding out, to carry the necessary extra crude petroleum.
If he means to build a pipeline, and he did not clarify that this afternoon, from Sarnia, that will only give Quebec another 50,000 barrels of crude petroleum a day. If he means to increase the capacity of the Interprovincial pipeline from Alberta through Saskatchewan to Sarnia in order to be able to supply the million barrels needed each day in eastern Canada, then of course he would have a project for which if he could get it off the tracing board, the Canadian consumers in that part of the country would have some appreciation. This government has sat idly by, failing to take any decision early enough to prevent a crisis here in Canada. In fact, I think they like the crisis.
I prepared some of these remarks before I heard the Prime Minister today. I ask what our policy should be on a short-term and long-term basis so Canada will not find itself in this position in the future. I am tired of saying there is no energy crisis in Canada, as we have a supply of natural gas and crude petroleum. What crisis there is is a government crisis as a result of procrastination and vacillation.

Secondly, we should create a tax climate that will encourage capital, particularly Canadian risk capital, into investment in exploration development of the Athabasca tar sands and to find other fields as we have done in the past. I heard the Prime Minister say this afternoon that it is not likely there are any other fields in Alberta. We should put together immediately a new national oil policy after consultation with the provinces and make certain that any surtax, a mechanism used to keep the price of gas and oil down in Canada when under pressure from high world competition and prices, will be returned to the provinces where the resource exists and is developed. I think that is a fair premise. I am sure that if you had a surtax on steel for some reason, that money should go back to the province of Ontario, or the money in respect of iron ore should go back to the province of Quebec where it is mined.
Surely that is a reasonable policy and we should be able to consult with the provinces and work out the problems. This Prime Minister, this government and the minister-I am happy to see him here in the House-have run slipshod over all the premiers of the provinces and provincial representatives.

speechtext: No way.

speechtext:
The hon. member should go and talk to the premiers. We should begin immediately, and this should have taken place years ago, to negotiate with the United States in reference to a natural gas pipeline down the Mackenzie delta, through Alberta to the industrial centres of Canada and the United States. Why would this be necessary? I agree with the Prime Minister in this regard. I prepared some of this before I listened to what he had to say.
The economics of bringing natural gas from the Arctic is such that we have to combine our efforts with the United States, which could then bring down its natural gas from their areas. The natural gas from both areas would be transported down the same pipeline. Our natural gas could be used in Canada and theirs could be used in their own country. That combined effort would make this energy economic and at a price range the people of Canada could afford. It would be at a price at which industries could use the energy and compete with world markets. As a result of the procrastination and vacillation of this government in not doing this years ago, we find this development has not taken place. This has been a government of words and inaction.
I know that some people are frightened because there is some mystery about the foreign investments bill which will set up a screening process, but no such process should

be used dictatorially by this government without consultation with the provinces that may be affected. I have talked to members from the Maritimes and I know that they need capital. Certain areas in western Canada need capital, but the needs may be entirely different than perhaps the needs in Ontario or in other parts of central Canada. Therefore, before the government uses this screening process there must be consultation with the provinces. Today we are self-sufficient in Canada, but if we have this kind of government which does everything to antagonize the development of the petroleum industry we will soon be in the position that other countries find themselves in, and have to rely on imports rather than on our own production.
We should now make certain that the Syncrude project, which is worth $800 million, guaranteeing 10,000 jobs and billions of barrels of crude petroleum for Canada in the future, goes ahead without frustration caused by scare tactics on the part of this government. The uncertainty and confusion in respect of government policy is frustrating and delaying this important project that promises a continued supply of energy for our industrial complexes and cheap fuel for our homes. This is an important project, but instead of the government providing incentives, it provides discouragements. The Premier of Alberta worked with a group for the development of the tar sands in order to guarantee a supply of crude petroleum not only in western Canada but here in eastern Canada.
The next thing I suggest is that we should return the National Energy Board to its proper function of being an independent board making decisions as to pipelines, security of supply, exports, imports, etc., and get government interference out of that board. In particular, the government must appoint men other than political heelers. I have read clauses of Bill C-236 that indicate this super-board the minister wants to set up will be able to override any decision of the Energy Board-and if that is not interference, nothing is.
The next question that came to my mind in considering this bill was why the future supply of petroleum and natural gas is so important to our well-being. May I set out now that according to recent technical papers, and this is material researched by an independent petroleum association, Canada is considered to have, at current rates of production, undiscovered reserves equivalent to 100 years' supply for oil needs and 250 years' supply for gas needs. In addition, and the Prime Minister touched on this today, the Alberta oil sands are estimated to contain 250 billion barrels of oil of which approximately 26.5 billion barrels are recoverable by current processes.

speechtext: Where do you get those figures?

speechtext:
The figures come from a report of the Canadian Petroleum Association, an independent petroleum group which hired technicians, geologists, to come up with these figures. While these potential reserves postulated by various geologists are large, they will only

become a reality by exploration, and only through risk exploration can Canada become assured of >
long-term supply. In undertaking this risk exploration it must first be recognized that compared to Middle East supplies or, in fact, any other reserves worldwide except the United States, Canadian oil and gas are high-cost in terms of finding, developing and transportation costs.
Wells in Venezuela produce as many as 10,000 barrels of crude per day. Our wells in Alberta, the best of them, produce about 100 to 200 barrels a day. It costs just as much to drill one of the wells in Alberta as it costs to drill wells in the Middle East or in Venezuela which produce 10,000 barrels a day. So the cost of our production is very high. Secondly, it must be recognized that these risk investments are generally of a fairly long-term nature in that there is a long lead time before an idea is transferred into reserves and possible return.
In central Canada it takes five to seven years to do the necessary geological, geophysical and drilling work required to develop a specific plan to start selling oil and gas. In the frontier area the lead time is even longer. Gas was found in Sable Island in 1967. There were close to 70 wells. Six years later this gas is still a considerable time from being produced. I heard in the House the other day, when the government was being questioned, that they were thinking of building a pipeline to get this gas into the Maritimes where it is needed. This should have been off the planning board a long time ago. The emergency is now; the winter is here; the people will be cold and will suffer now.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext: You said there is no crisis.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
There is a government crisis, but no shortage of supply. Gas was found at Drake Point in the Arctic in July, 1969, and it is unlikely that any gas will be marketed before the 1980s. The point I wish to make is that these long lead time periods require committing funds for a considerable period into the future, with little or no return. Each long-term commitment necessitates long-term planning and the careful evaluation of alternatives, particularly when the need for capital is so great.
All we have had from this government is short-term planning, which is not good enough. When they talk about the crisis, the crisis is because there is no transportation policy or encouragement in respect of a transportation policy. Therefore, we have a crisis now in Quebec and in the Maritimes. From the individual company's point of view, the exploration risk must be weighed against opportunities elsewhere. I could name many companies which have their head office in Calgary and which are not drilling in Alberta or becoming involved in the tar sands. They have gone to the North Sea because they get a better deal from the British.
The oil industry is a multinational industry because risk capital flows all over the world. That is why it takes a lot of capital to develop and find either oil or natural gas. The industry needs to work in a climate of relatively stable conditions. That is why I endorse the Energy Board. It cannot operate in a legislative vacuum such as it does under this government. It cannot operate under conditions
Energy Supplies Emergency Act where great uncertainties exist, or in circumstances where legislative or regulatory guarantees are unilaterally changed without regard to the guarantee. That is exactly what Bill C-236 will do. It will create a czar in the government which will be all powerful in respect of energy, and the board will have to carry out the orders of the great general. The industry cannot operate where legislative changes are made retroactively or where legislative changes are made quickly without allowing for a phase-in period to allow industry adjustments.
May I repeat that if the transportation facilities were adequate, Canada would be self-sufficient in energy supplies and the consumers this winter would not be frightened about the possibility of not being warm in their homes and in the hospitals. I heard that in one hospital, I believe it was in the province of Newfoundland, several deaths of babies occurred because of the cold-and this in a place like Canada!

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That was on television. You may say it is nonsense. Until recently, Arab nations provided to eastern Canada 30 per cent of its crude oil needs. This amounted to approximately 300,000 barrels of crude oil a day. The government maintained that the Arabs were going to cut back 25 per cent of that supply, amounting to 75,000 barrels of crude oil a day. Now the government maintains the shortage will be not 75,000 barrels a day but 200,000 barrels a day. They maintain that this is due to the multinational oil companies having the power to argue and successfully allege that the contracts for supply of this crude petroleum can be upset due to impossibility of performance of supply contracts.
It is they that are on the side of the multinational corporations. They say they cannot do anything about it. They say they are helpless. This has been given the fancy term force majeure, a clause in the contract relieving these oil companies from fulfilling their contracts. EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTED INVITATION TO SAUDIAN ARABIAN AND ALGERIAN OIL MINISTERS TO VISIT CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) to give consideration to inviting Sheik Yamani, oil minister of Saudi Arabia, to come to Ottawa. I noted that the Saudi minister and his Algerian counterpart were in the United States after completing visits to western Europe.
In the whole confused story of our energy problem there is at least one aspect that is clear. We are not in meaningful communication with great portions of the Arab world, especially the major oil producers. One day we have announcements of actions by Saudi Arabia. The next day we are told that not Saudi Arabia but Abu Dhabi was involved. There is no clearcut picture of Canada's status in reference to oil coming from the Portland pipeline. We have been told that all was well, and well understood. I heard Sheik Yamani on television a few days ago indicate that that aspect would need looking into.
A leading oil man declares that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) was advised that Saudi Arabia had Canada on the embargo list. The minister denied this but was unable to indicate how much oil had been shipped from Saudi Arabia to Canada in the last 30 days. Indeed, the whole record of the minister's handling of the present problem is so inept as to be frightening. On Tuesday, the Come-By-Chance announcement was an "ace in the hole". On Wednesday, it was something considerably less. On an issue of such seriousness, with profound ramifications, economic, constitutional and international, the people of this country should not be placed in such jeopardy as to have their destinies reside in a man whose incapacity has been so painfully proven over many years in so many public assignments.
I hoped the Secretary of State for External Affairs would follow my suggestion and arrange that Sheik Yamani be invited to Ottawa so that some information and clarity might be obtained. I would like to know if the Sheik was invited. As long ago as last spring I urged, in the external affairs committee, the necessity of opening full-fledged diplomatic missions in the oil states of the Arab world. With the vast areas of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the Gulf states we have either no diplomatic contact or contact of the most tenuous kind. Missions in Cairo, Beirut, and Tel Aviv scarcely open the line of communication with oil states. Iraq has a most highly qualified ambassador in Ottawa, but we seem not able to open a mission in Baghdad.
Although the problems and burdens likely to fall upon the ordinary Canadian citizen, especially in the Atlantic region, are of the utmost importance, we must not lose sight of the fact that the current Canadian problem about

December 6, 1973
Adjournment Debate
oil, whatever its dimensions, cannot be considered today in isolation from the highly explosive Middle East political and military situation.
Little is gained by denouncing the Arab states, whose newly proven unity has been most effective, as practitioners of blackmail. The use of economic sanctions has an ancient history. Long ago it was used by combatants and opponents. In recent years I have heard Canadian ministers point with pious pride to our non-trade with Rhodesia. Then we think of the Trading with the Enemy Act of the United States and the moral satisfaction of those Canadians who dilate upon the sinfulness of buying California grapes.
There is no law, international or otherwise, which decrees that the Arabs must sell their oil indiscriminately all over the world. I must regret that they have taken any steps to inhibit in any degree their sales to my country, but I do not deny them the right to select their customers in the international marketplace.
In reference to the over-all political situation, Mr. Speaker, I think the Canadian people have a right to know just where we stand with the Arab world. Have we reasons for quarrelling with these people? Why is Canada in a category different from that of Britain, France, Belgium and other European countries? What view do we have on the Middle East situation differing from these countries? They recognize Israel, and ipso facto believe in its existence. Does Canada believe that the lands occupied by Israel after the UN decision of the forties and the 1967 war are to be permanently alienated from the Arab states? Is this the reason why Canada is on the neutral list and our NATO allies in Europe, with two exceptions, are on the friendly list? This is a very important and significant question.
I think that we should know what is the stand of the government on this most volatile and very grave portentous situation. The reasons for our being in a category different from Britain and France should be made clear to the people of Canada who may suffer grievously. All of these countries supported UN resolution 242, as did we. Wherein have we differed since? For what reason are we on less than friendly terms with the Arab world, with whom we have had no conflicts or quarrels so far as I know, and whose progress toward a peaceful, prosperous existence we should welcome?
I would welcome some replies from the distinguished parliamentary secretary for whom I have the highest regard, and indeed I may have the honour of getting a reply from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who is famous for presenting the worst possible situations. With his record, I would say he is the best possible man to tell us about another worst possible situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTED INVITATION TO SAUDIAN ARABIAN AND ALGERIAN OIL MINISTERS TO VISIT CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to reply to the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) who is generally well regarded in this House, although not for any particular intellectual qualifications. I think he is generally regarded as being a rather well meaning, but very shallow and intellectually light-

weight person. Still it is certainly a pleasure to reply to him. I may also say the most outstanding thing about the hon. member is his sideburns, in respect of which no other member of the House can claim precedence. He has, undoubtedly, the most outstanding pair of sideburns in the House.
I was interested in his reference to Sheik Yamani, and that gave me greater pleasure in rising to speak tonight because I had the most recent opportunity of any member of the House to speak with the sheik, who was a classmate of mine at Harvard law school. The sheik made it very clear to me at the time, and I have since vouchsafed it to this House, that Canada is on no embargo list so far as his government is concerned, and indeed the suggestions to that effect by the hon. member for Hillsborough and other badly informed persons like the hon. member are, of course, without foundation.
I welcome the statement of the sheik that in fact he had the highest regard for our country and that he did not share the impression which the hon. member for Hillsborough sought to circulate this evening, that Canada is poorly regarded in the Arab world. Indeed, Canada is well regarded, and so far as the sheik is concerned, he said he would check this rumour, created by an international petroleum corporation as to the way in which it would have the Arab peoples view us.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that it is indeed in the interests of Canada and Canadians to establish good relations with the Arab peoples and this has been one of the objectives of our foreign policy for many years. This has been a difficult relationship in terms of both the Arab and Israeli communities, and this is why Canadians above all have sought to play a role that would not aggravate either side of the controversy. Quite to the contrary, Canadians want to play a constructive role so that these two peoples, arising from such close ethnic backgrounds, with so many ties of history, can come together and establish a lasting and permanent peace on the basis of mutual co-operation and confidence in the Middle East.
The hon. member referred to many of the hard fought debates in the United Nations General Assembly on the question of the ceasefire lines, on resolution 242 and on other matters. I would say, Mr. Speaker, in this regard that the important question for Canadians to face, even though Canadians may at the moment be somewhat concerned about oil supplies, about the lack of oil, or extent of deprivation from which they suffer or with which they may be threatened, is the question of the importance of establishing in the Middle East community an effective role for Canadians to play in trying to bring those two communities together.
This has been the role of the government of Canada, dating back, if I may say so, to the days of my former leader whom the hon. member for Hillsborough was prepared to castigate in the past, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson. The work of that great Canadian in the Middle East was recognized. It was known that he wanted to try and bring about peace between those two great and historic peoples. This is the role for Canada. This is the role this government will try to discharge, Mr. Speaker.
December 6, 1973

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROTECTION OF CANADIAN VISITORS TO UNITED STATES AGAINST BEING STRANDED IF GAS RATIONING INTRODUCED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak tonight because of my failure last Monday to persuade the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) to even acknowledge his responsibility for protecting the well-being of Canadian citizens who may soon be stranded in the United States if gasoline rationing is invoked in that country. Hansard records my questions and the minister's evasions and blandishments in the following way, at page 8343:

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROTECTION OF CANADIAN VISITORS TO UNITED STATES AGAINST BEING STRANDED IF GAS RATIONING INTRODUCED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It arises from the possibility of gasoline rationing in the United States. Has the minister consulted with his American counterparts to get an agreement from the Americans to ensure that the interests of Canadians abroad will be protected so they will not be stranded there if gasoline rationing is introduced in that country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROTECTION OF CANADIAN VISITORS TO UNITED STATES AGAINST BEING STRANDED IF GAS RATIONING INTRODUCED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not think that Canadians who wish to travel in the United States would be exempted from those kinds of measures. I should think they would want to comply.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROTECTION OF CANADIAN VISITORS TO UNITED STATES AGAINST BEING STRANDED IF GAS RATIONING INTRODUCED
speechtext: What specific measures will the minister be taking on behalf of the Canadian government to protect the interests of Canadian nationals travelling abroad who find themselves trapped there? Is the minister not concerned about the interests of Canadian?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROTECTION OF CANADIAN VISITORS TO UNITED STATES AGAINST BEING STRANDED IF GAS RATIONING INTRODUCED
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we are concerned. I think we can look after the interests of Canadians in this regard. However, I do not think we should create the impression that we should be free when Americans are subject to rationing.
What a remarkable statement for a minister of the Crown to make-that he did not feel Canadians trapped in the United States as a result of American rationing would want any special treatment if it were necessary to get them home to their families. I cannot help but be reminded, when I read the comments of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, of Winston Churchill's description of Clement Attlee as "a sheep in sheep's clothing".
This year, tens of thousands of Canadians will be visiting the United States and will be taking with them millions of tourist dollars which will be a great asset to the American economy. The only thing they ask in return from the Americans is that they be treated in a fair and decent way, and that they not be left stranded hundreds of miles from their homes and families. I think their request is not unreasonable. Yet, the minister refuses even to talk to the Americans to request that the rights of Canadians be respected. Although he intimates that the government can do something for stranted Canadians, he refuses to say what.
This is the second time since the beginning of the energy crisis that this minister has demonstrated to Canadians that you will find more backbone in a bowl of jello than you will find in his office. It was not all that long ago that we saw on nationwide television the rather pathetic spectacle of the Secretary of State for External
Adjournment Debate
Affairs begging the ambassadors of the Arab sheikhs not to blackmail this country with their oil. "We like the Israelis" he said, "but we also like the Arabs too. We want to be everybody's friend and we know that everybody will want to be our friends too."
That performance, Mr. Speaker, did not fill Canadians with pride. They were not proud to see their government jumping through Arab hoops in order to be ensured that our oil supply is not cut. In the end, Canada has still been subject to the Arab cutback in production. It is countries like Holland and the United States, which refused to be blackmailed away from support of Israel, which have reason for pride. Yet, unlike Canada, both those countries are highly dependent on oil from the Middle East for the health of their respective economies. This country, which is one of the few major nations in the world able to claim self-sufficiency in oil, refuses even to make a protest over the hostile and aggressive actions of the Arabs against us.
It appears, Mr. Speaker, that this coalition government will continue in office for some months. However, as long as this minister retains his portfolio, we will continue to pay for his timidity with the honour and the rights of Canadians.
